Katharina von Schlegel
kah-tah-REE-nah fon SHLAY-gul
proper noun
Katharina, from the Greek Aikaterine, traditionally rendered “pure”; von Schlegel, a German noble surname.

📖 Biblical Definition

Katharina von Schlegel (born 1697) was a German hymn-writer of the Pietist era, associated with the devout court circles of Cothen, whose verse flowed out of the German Lutheran piety that prized heartfelt devotion to Christ and quiet trust in His providence. She is known to the English-speaking church almost entirely through one hymn, “Be Still, My Soul,” which was carried into English by a later translator and wedded to the noble tune Finlandia. The hymn is a sustained counsel to the troubled believer to be still and rest in the Lord, for He remains faithful through every grief and loss; it bids the soul leave to God the ordering of its way, trusting that the One who ruled the wind and waves still governs the storms of providence. It looks beyond the sorrows of this life to the day when grief is past and the believer shall meet at last the Savior face to face, when disappointment, grief, and fear are gone, when love’s purest joys restored shall be. Rooted in the Psalmist’s command to be still and know that God is God, the hymn is a confession of the sovereignty and faithfulness of God over all the affairs of His people. Through it Katharina von Schlegel has taught generations of afflicted saints to hand their cares to a faithful Father and to wait in stillness for His sure deliverance.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A German Pietist hymn-writer (born 1697), author of “Be Still, My Soul.”

expand to see more

KATHARINA VON SCHLEGEL, a German Lutheran hymn-writer of the Pietist era (born 1697).

Associated with the devout court circles of Cöthen in Germany.

Wrote the hymn known in English as “Be Still, My Soul.”

The hymn was later translated into English and set to the tune “Finlandia.”

It counsels the troubled soul to rest in God’s faithfulness and providence (Psa 46:10).

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 46:10 — "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."

Psa 37:7 — "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass."

Mar 4:39 — "And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm."

Isa 26:3 — "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The truth to recover is stillness grounded in God’s sovereignty and faithfulness — not a vague self-soothing, but rest in the God who rules the storm.

expand to see more

Here a real misuse may be named. “Be Still, My Soul” is sometimes pressed into a generic mood of calm, a kind of self-administered serenity divorced from its object. But the stillness Schlegel sings is commanded by the Psalm’s ground: “Be still, and know that I am God.” The peace is not in quieting oneself but in trusting the sovereign, faithful Lord who orders every providence.

Recover the hymn by recovering its God. Its comfort is that the same Christ who said “Peace, be still” to the sea still governs the believer’s storms, and that beyond every grief lies the certain meeting with the Savior face to face. Loosed from that confidence, the hymn becomes mere sentiment; anchored to it, it is a strong tower for the afflicted soul.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The hymn’s title and theme rest on the Psalmist’s command to be still and know that God is God.

expand to see more

Katharina von Schlegel — Katharina, from the Greek, traditionally “pure.”

“Be still” renders the Hebrew raphah, to let go, cease striving (Psa 46:10).

“Peace, be still” quotes the Lord’s word to the sea in Mark 4:39.

“Rest in the LORD” echoes Psalm 37:7.

The English version was made by Jane Borthwick and set to Sibelius’ “Finlandia.”

Usage

"Katharina von Schlegel taught the troubled soul to be still and rest in God’s providence."

"Through one hymn, Katharina von Schlegel has comforted generations of afflicted saints."

"Katharina von Schlegel grounded her counsel of stillness in the sovereignty of God."
